newsitem.title: UK: Dlr settles just under 1.64 marks at European close.
newsitem.headline: Dlr settles just under 1.64 marks at European close.

text.p: The dollar stormed to its highest level here in more than 2-1/2 years against the German mark and almost four years against the yen as U.S., European and Japanese authorities appeared to give its recent rally a green light. The U.S. unit succumbed to some mild profit-taking later in the day as U.S. stocks and bonds also pared some of their recent gains. Bundesbank member Ernst Welteke also help keep a lid on it as he cautioned about the pace of recent mark depreciation.

However, analysts remained bullish on the dollar outlook against European currencies in particular. "There's an underlying feeling that no one in power is unhappy with the extent of the dollar's rise, although the pace may be seen as a little excessive," said Adrian Schmidt, economist at Chase Investment Bank. "In the absence of any complaint from G7 (Group of Seven industrialised nations), the dollar still looks good on the basis of attractive rates in a market searching for yield." At 1630 GMT, the dollar was trading at 1.6390/95 marks compared with 1.6242/52 late Tuesday but off a 31-month high at 1.6455 set early in Europe. Dollar/yen was at 118.90/119.00 compared with 117.82/87 late yesterday. The dollar set a 47-month high at 119.20 yen early in the session and a 32-month high at 1.4360 Swiss francs. The dollar has risen more than 10 pfennigs, or as much as 6.9 percent, against the mark since the beginning of this year alone as bond yield spreads between the U.S. and Europe widened sharply in favour of the dollar. Despite the sharp dollar rise this year, which has seen a 2.9 percent rise against the yen. U.S. Treasury secretary Robert Rubin re-iterated overnight his long-standing foreign exchange policy that a strong dollar is in the interests of the U.S. European and Japan officials did little to contradict that. The dollar got a further lift from reports that Bank of France governor Jean-Claude Trichet said the G7 endorsed the dollar rise and would be happy to see it rise further. Japanese Minister of Finance Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said he believed the G7 backed the U.S. strong-dollar policy. "The U.S. has been saying that it is seeking a strong dollar. My understanding is that the G7 nations share that stance." The G7 finance ministers meet in Berlin on February 8. One note of caution came later. The Bundesbank's Welteke said the mark, also falling against neighbouring European currencies, could not continue to slide at the pace seen in recent days. Nevertheless, Welteke said the dollar's rise had no inflationary implications and would be good for German exports, the only "ray of light" for German economic growth. "The market is not yet overly long of dollars but is increasingly happy getting paid, in terms of interest rate pick-up, for doing what the authorities are happy with," said Avinash Persaud, head of currency research at JP Morgan in Europe. "The U.S. is happy to see the higher dollar bear down on any imported inflation, while the Bundesbank knows the German economy needs the export boost." Falling interest rates across Europe also helps. The Bank of Italy cut its discount rate by three-quarters of a percentage point to 6.75 percent late on Tuesday, partly in response to the lira's strength against the mark. The low European interest rate story was reinforced by the latest German economic data. The Bundesbank revised November industrial orders data down, and the Ifo research institute said on Tuesday its December business sentiment index fell. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's speech on Tuesday kept the prospect of higher U.S. interest rates alive, but his sanguine view of growth and inflation kept stock and bonds steady. --London newsroom +44 171 542 6762
